title: The Man in Linen and the War Behind History
summary: In the third year of Cyrus, after three weeks of mourning and fasting, Daniel sees a dazzling man dressed in linen by the Tigris River and collapses. A heavenly messenger strengthens him and explains that he was delayed for twenty-one days by the prince of the kingdom of Persia until Michael came to help. He has come to tell Daniel what will happen to his people in the latter days, and he must return to fight the princes of Persia and Greece.
story: Chapters 10 to 12 form a single, final vision, the longest in the book, and chapter 10 is its prologue. The exiles have been free to go home for about two years, and some have gone, but the book gives no sign that Daniel went with them. The news from Jerusalem was not good: the returned community was small and poor, and opposition had stalled the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 4:1-5, 24). Daniel is mourning. What he receives in reply is not a quick fix but a glimpse behind history. The conflicts of empires that chapter 11 will describe are shown to have a hidden, spiritual dimension, and God's people have a heavenly champion in them. The chapter prepares Daniel, and the reader, to hear hard news about the centuries ahead.
historical:
The third year of Cyrus king of Persia is about 536 BC, counting from his conquest of Babylon in 539 BC. It is the latest date in the book. Daniel would have been in his eighties, some seventy years after he was taken to Babylon as a youth (1:1-6). Cyrus had allowed the exiles to return and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1-4), and a first group under Sheshbazzar and later Zerubbabel had gone back. The foundations of the temple were laid, but work soon halted under local opposition and was not resumed until the reign of Darius I, around 520 BC (Ezra 4 to 6).

Daniel sees the vision on the bank of the Tigris, which runs east of the Euphrates through Mesopotamia; the Hebrew calls it by its ancient name, Hiddekel, the same name used for one of the rivers of Eden (Genesis 2:14). The messenger's reference to the prince of Greece (verse 20) looks ahead to the rise of Alexander the Great, who conquered the Persian Empire in the 330s BC. Those who date the book to the second century BC read the chapter as the introduction to a survey of history written from the time of Antiochus IV; those who hold the traditional date read it as genuine foresight granted to Daniel in the Persian period.
cultural:
Daniel's three weeks of mourning involved giving up rich food, meat, wine, and the olive oil people rubbed on their skin in a hot, dry climate. It was a partial fast, a deliberate setting aside of comforts. The date he gives, the twenty-fourth of the first month (Nisan, in spring), means the fast ran through the season of Passover and Unleavened Bread, the feasts that remembered the exodus. Daniel spent the festival of liberation in mourning, perhaps over the slow and struggling return.

The man in linen is described in terms drawn from Israel's worship and from earlier prophetic visions. Linen was the garment of priests (Leviticus 16:4) and of the heavenly scribe in Ezekiel 9. His appearance, like beryl, lightning, torches, polished bronze, and the sound of a multitude, recalls Ezekiel's vision of the glory of God (Ezekiel 1). The idea that nations have heavenly princes over them reflects a belief found elsewhere in the Old Testament, where God assigns the nations their borders and places them under heavenly beings (Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek translation; Psalm 82). Michael, whose name means who is like God, is here the prince of Israel.
literary: The chapter is built around Daniel's weakness and three touches that restore him. He sees the vision and loses all strength (verses 7-9); a hand touches him and sets him on hands and knees (verse 10); one like a man touches his lips so that he can speak (verse 16); and a final touch strengthens him to hear (verses 18-19). Twice he is called highly precious and told not to fear (verses 11-12 and 19). The narrative slows deliberately, building tension before the revelation begins in 11:2. The messenger's speech also frames the vision's content: the conflict with Persia and then Greece in the heavenly realm (10:20-21) matches the earthly history of Persia and Greece that follows. Reading 10:1 to 12:13 as one unit is essential; the chapter breaks are later additions and cut the vision into pieces.

outline.t: The man dressed in linen by the Tigris
The coming fight with the princes of Persia and Greece

doctrines.note: The chapter lifts the curtain on history and shows that the rise and fall of empires is not the whole story. There is conflict in the unseen realm, yet the messenger speaks from the Book of Truth: what will happen is already known to God.

Daniel's words were heard from the first day he humbled himself (verse 12), though the answer took three weeks to arrive. The delay did not mean God had not heard. Scripture does not explain the mechanics of this spiritual resistance, and wise readers do not build detailed systems on it.

Seeing God's messenger overwhelms Daniel. Revelation is not something humans master; Daniel can receive it only because he is touched, strengthened, and given speech. God stoops to make his word bearable to weak people.

words.note: Sar, prince, ruler, or commander. The word is used for human officials throughout the Old Testament, but here it names the spiritual powers associated with Persia and Greece and with Israel (Michael, one of the chief princes). The same word links the earthly and heavenly realms, suggesting that the struggles of nations have a spiritual side.

Michael, who is like God. Daniel is the first book to name him, as one of the chief princes and Israel's own prince (verse 21; 12:1). The New Testament calls him the archangel (Jude 9) and pictures him fighting the dragon (Revelation 12:7).

Chamudah, something desirable or precious. Daniel is called a man highly precious, literally a man of precious things, here and in 9:23. The word elsewhere describes treasures and fine goods. God's messenger comes to a frightened old man and tells him that he is treasured.

christ: The man in linen of verses 5-6 reappears, almost detail for detail, in John's vision of the risen Christ in Revelation 1:13-15: clothed in a long robe with a gold sash, eyes like blazing fire, feet like polished bronze, and a voice like many waters. Some Christian interpreters have therefore identified the man in Daniel 10 as an appearance of the Son of God before his incarnation; others think he is an angel, perhaps Gabriel, since the one who speaks in verses 12-14 needed Michael's help. Either way, John uses Daniel's language to show that the glory Daniel could not bear belongs to Jesus. The pattern of the chapter also anticipates the gospel: a heavenly figure touches a fallen man and tells him not to be afraid (compare Revelation 1:17), and the New Testament teaches that Christ has triumphed over the rulers and authorities that oppose God's people (Colossians 2:15).

hard.q: Are there really spiritual princes over nations, and could an angel be delayed?
hard.a:
The chapter speaks plainly of a prince of Persia who resisted God's messenger for twenty-one days and a prince of Greece still to come, and it presents Michael as Israel's prince. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take these as spiritual beings, not human rulers, because they fight alongside and against angels. This fits other biblical texts that speak of heavenly beings associated with the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8 in its older textual form; Psalm 82) and Paul's language about rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms (Ephesians 6:12).

Readers differ on how far to press the details. Some take the chapter as a literal description of territorial spirits and draw practical lessons for prayer and spiritual warfare. Others caution that apocalyptic writing uses vivid pictures to reveal the spiritual significance of historical events, and that the text says nothing about how people should identify or engage such powers. What the chapter clearly teaches is that history has an unseen dimension, that God's purposes meet real resistance, and that the resistance does not prevail. The messenger comes, Daniel is strengthened, and the Book of Truth is read out.

questions: Daniel's prayer was heard on the first day, but the answer came three weeks later. How do you usually interpret the delay of an answer to prayer?
The messenger touches Daniel three times before he is able to hear. What has God used to strengthen you when the truth felt too heavy to bear?
The chapter suggests that the conflicts of nations have a spiritual dimension. How might that change the way Christians think and pray about the powers of their own day?
